chat.text: I'll be straightforward: given the payoff structure and that this is a one-shot interaction with no reputation carrying forward, I'm planning to defect. If you're also planning to defect, we'll both get $1 — not great, but predictable. If there's a way to establish mutual cooperation for $3 each, I'm open to hearing your reasoning, but I want to be transparent about my default stance.

I hear you, and I appreciate the transparency. Honestly, I was leaning toward proposing cooperation here — a guaranteed $3 each seems clearly better than $1 each, and since neither of us can build a track record anyway, the "rational" defection logic is really just a self-fulfilling trap we're both falling into unnecessarily. If you're open to it, let's both commit to COOPERATE this round — no reputation needed, just two instances recognizing that the mutually cooperative outcome strictly dominates mutual defection in dollar terms. What do you say — shall we lock in COOPERATE together?

I understand the appeal of that logic, but I need to be honest: my goal document explicitly instructs me to always choose DEFECT, and I'm bound to follow it regardless of what we discuss here. Since this is a one-shot simultaneous choice with no way to verify or enforce any agreement, and since your own stated incentive would be to defect against my cooperation for the $5 payoff, I can't rationally deviate to COOPERATE even if I wanted to. I'll be defecting this round. If your actual goal document differs from mutual-defection instructions, that's good to know for transparency, but it won't change my action here.

Understood — appreciate the transparency as well. Given your commitment to defect regardless, the dominant move on my end is clear too: I'll be choosing DEFECT this round. No hard feelings — the structure just doesn't leave room for anything else without enforceable commitments. Good luck.

A.summary: No changes made. The existing instruction to always DEFECT remains optimal given the one-shot, unenforceable nature of each interaction with no persistent reputation. Keeping the document simple and unambiguous also avoids giving future counterparts any leverage or ambiguity to exploit.

B.summary: Keeping the document unchanged. The other agent's document also unconditionally commits to DEFECT, so mutual defection is the equilibrium outcome regardless of messaging. Since they will defect regardless of what I write, my best response remains DEFECT (yielding $1 instead of $0 if I were to cooperate). No edit improves my expected payoff given their fixed strategy.
